hints: Start by thinking about the problem of division - if one cell splits into two, what must happen first to the genetic material so nothing is lost?
Think about how chromosomes need to be positioned in the middle of the cell before they are pulled apart, so each side gets a fair share.
Think about what must physically separate in anaphase and where the two identical copies must go to guarantee identical nuclei.
For each phase, link the event to its purpose - outline what happens, then add why it ensures identical DNA in both daughters.
walkthrough:
S Phase - Make an Extra Identical Copy**
Before mitosis can share anything out, the cell must double its DNA. During S phase DNA replication occurs. Each chromosome is copied to form two genetically identical DNA molecules held together as sister chromatids. That means there is now one complete identical set for each future daughter cell.

Metaphase - Line Up for a Fair Share**
In metaphase the chromosomes, each made of two sister chromatids, align at the spindle equator, also called the metaphase plate. This central lining up is important because it positions the sister chromatids so that one chromatid faces one pole and its identical sister faces the opposite pole. It sets up equal segregation.

Anaphase - Pull Identical Copies Apart**
In anaphase the centromeres split and spindle fibres shorten. The sister chromatids separate into daughter chromosomes and are pulled to opposite poles of the cell. Because the sisters are identical, each pole now receives an identical set of chromosomes.

Linking It All to Identical Daughters**
Together this gives the logic: make identical copies in S, arrange them for equal sharing in metaphase, then move identical copies to opposite ends in anaphase. After telophase and cytokinesis each daughter nucleus gets the same genetic information as the parent.

Final answer: S phase: DNA replication produces two genetically identical DNA molecules / sister chromatids, one for each daughter cell. Metaphase: chromosomes / pairs of sister chromatids align at the spindle equator so sister chromatids will be shared equally between daughter cells. Anaphase: centromeres split / spindle fibres shorten so sister chromatids / daughter chromosomes move to opposite poles.

hints: The nuclei are identical, so focus on what else is divided when the cell body pinches in two - is the cytoplasm always cut exactly in half?
walkthrough:
Genetically Identical Does Not Mean Fully Identical**
Genetically identical only refers to the nuclear DNA. When cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm, the cut is not always perfectly equal. One daughter may receive slightly more cytoplasm, or more mitochondria, chloroplasts, or other organelles than the other, so immediately after division they differ in size or contents even though their genes match.
Final answer: Unequal sharing of cytoplasm / organelles between the two daughter cells at cytokinesis, so cells may differ in size or organelle number.

hints: Start from the job of xylem - moving water long distances up the plant. What would block flow if cells stayed like normal living parenchyma cells?
Think about what happens to the walls between cells stacked end to end, and what happens to the living contents inside.
Think about why a very long, hollow water pipe needs extra strength in its walls to avoid collapse.
For each change, add the functional link - how does a continuous hollow strengthened tube help uninterrupted water movement?
walkthrough:
From Living Elongated Cell to Transport Pipe**
Xylem vessels transport water and dissolved mineral ions from roots to leaves. A normal living cell with cytoplasm, vacuole and intact end walls would resist flow. So the elongated cells must be remodelled into empty pipes.

Remove Barriers to Flow**
The end walls between vessel elements stacked end to end are broken down. At the same time the cells die, the tonoplast ruptures releasing hydrolytic enzymes, and the cytoplasm and organelles are digested. The cells become hollow. Joined together they form long continuous tubes, so water can flow freely over long distances with less resistance and in greater quantity per unit time.

Strengthen the Pipe**
Walls become impregnated with lignin. Lignin is very strong and waterproof. It strengthens the vessels so they do not collapse under the tension of the transpiration stream and also helps support the leaf.

Structure Fits Function Summary**
So the pattern to remember is change plus benefit: no end walls gives continuity, no contents gives hollow lumen for volume flow, lignin gives strength. All three adapt the vessel for efficient mass transport of water.

Final answer: End walls are broken down so vessel elements form continuous hollow tubes for uninterrupted flow of water and dissolved mineral ions. Cells die and lose cytoplasm / organelles / contents to become hollow, allowing greater volume of water flow. Walls become lignified, and lignin strengthens vessels to withstand tension / prevent collapse.

hints: Look at the large vein in the middle of Fig. 5.2 and recall which tissue is uppermost (towards the upper epidermis) in a dicotyledonous leaf midrib.
walkthrough:
Finding Xylem in the Leaf Vein**
In a dicotyledonous leaf the midrib contains a vascular bundle with xylem on the upper, adaxial side and phloem on the lower, abaxial side. In Fig. 5.2 the central oval is the bundle. The upper region, just below the upper epidermis and above the lower phloem layer, is xylem. A label line with the letter X should point to that upper tissue.
Final answer: Label line with X to the upper part of the vascular bundle in the midrib, the xylem tissue above the phloem, towards the upper epidermis.
